paragraphs.text: Chapter 6. Focus

Our ability to get and stay motivated, to focus, and to learn new things is at the heart of what it is to be successful in life. Not just in school and work, but in creative endeavors and athletics. Consider the effort it takes to study for a big test or remember the material needed for a big presentation, or even Stick with a new approach to a painting or new musical instrument practice, or try to respond to a social situation in a new way. The question then becomes, "How?" How can we get motivated when our energy or natural impulses pull us toward apathy, overthinking, or procrastination? How can we tap into heightened focus, on demand? How can we learn faster and more effectively? It turns out these are states of mind and body that we can learn to deliberately access. My second year of college is when I first started to discover this. I learned that motivation can happen automatically as the consequence of, say, being excited or intrigued by something but it can also be deliberately fostered. As I mentioned a bit in the introduction, I went from being a good student in my early life to falling behind my peers in high school. I touched on Why that happened, but I make no excuses. Those were ultimately my own choices and actions. And those challenges both in and out of school, and watching my peers face those challenges too—seeing some soar and thrive while others struggled—would all become

a blessing in many ways. It forced me to realize that no one was coming to save me and that I had to change things on my own. That realization scared me, but it's what motivated me to turn my life around. I never quite had the exact words for what went through my head at that moment until recently, when a very wise friend and mentor said something and I thought, "THAT! That's what I was hearing in my head! THAT!" I can't say I came up with it, but it's something that I have heard in my head in fragments, over and over since I was nineteen. I Still remind myself of it every day: Losers take the negative things that happen to them and the feelings that come from things that suck... and they wallow and they use itfor self- or outward destruction. Winners however take whatever they feel—even if it sucks—and they transmute those feelings into actions that are good for themselves and for the world. I chose to do something. And through that choice, I learned that while motivation can result in action, it's possible for action to result in motivation too. As a sophomore in college, I decided to study as if my life depended on it. I didn't care if I liked the subject. I decided it made no difference, that eventually I would find the right path if I kept moving forward but I was going to move forward no matter what. Sure enough, my motivation to learn grew more and more, and morphed into a desire to get a PhD in a topic I fell in love with, to run a lab, to teach, and to build a career in science. Somewhere early along the way that fear I described dissipated. My love of certain topics and

You are asking your brain to change, and your brain doesn't want to change. Changing is very energetically demanding for brains. This uncomfortable feeling is something I often refer to as "limbic friction." It's not an oficial scientific term, but it refers to a state of elevated autonomic arousal where you're funneling into focus, and it takes constant or near-constant effort to get there and stay there. It's a mental edge of sorts. Once I understood that this limbic friction was not only normal, but essential, focus and learning became easier. I started seeking it out. And it felt good. I share this backstory simply to help illustrate that motivation, focus, and learning are states of mind and body. They have neural and hormonal underpinnings, much in the same way that REM sleep has its neural and hormonal underpinnings, as does stress, and so on. And that's good news, because it makes what might otherwise be nebulous, clear. We know what to aim for. This is a physiology-first approach to focus, motivation, and learning. It's rooted in how we work, which is Why the approach works. In this chapter you'll learn how to enhance your ability to focus by leveraging that. You'll also learn a powerful tool for "getting motivated" that is unlike all others you've likely seen before. And you'll finally get the truth about neuroplasticity —the rewiring of neural circuits that underlies all forms of learning (and forgetting), and that is often referred to simply as plasticity. Most everyone has heard of plasticity but honestly, most of the ways I've seen it discussed publicly are flat-out wrong. Perhaps you've heard that "Every experience you have changes your brain." That is not true. Or

"It takes twenty-one days to form a new habit." Wrong again. It can take a few days or a year, based on your level of motivation. Perhaps you've heard that "Your brain makes new neurons for your entire life." (The oficial terrn for that is neurogenesis.) Alas, barely any new neurons are added to the brain after puberty except for in your olfactory system, which allows you to smell, and those are mostly to replace neurons you've Iost. Starting to get depressed? Well don't, because despite these myths, we all possess a tremendous ability to rewire our brains and to learn at any age. The key is to understand the type of plasticity you're after. What we're talking about here—the rewiring of our brains that occurs as part of learning at any age—is a process that involves a specific set of steps that must be completed in a specific sequencefor learning to occur. I call these steps self-directed adaptive plasticity (SDAP). Mastering these steps opens the doors to learning pretty much anything you set your mind to. And that's what this chapter is about. The Steps and Sequence of SDAP Let's start with an overview of how SDAP occurs: Get alert. SDAP requires you to focus on the material at hand. Alertness sets the stage for focus; it's a precursor. 1'11 explain all this in the pages ahead. So get alert and.. Get and stay focused.

Focused on what? On implementing a specific strategy during your learning bout. As yougo... Maintain a state of urgency. Your internal state really matters as you learn. You can't be too relaxed, but you can't be stressed either. I define a state of urgency as simply a state of persistent motivation. It's the state to aim for because it has you stay alert but not too alert and.. Embrace errors. Errors that arise from genuine attempts to do something are key signals for triggering plasticity. Your nervous system is stimulated to rewire largely based on what you fail to do, not what you do correctly. Rest. Sleep is when neural rewiring actually occurs, especially during REM sleep the first night after a learning bout. There are other ways you can incorporate rest—like non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and short breaks—to improve performance. Repeat. Consolidate newly learned material or skills through repeat performance, either through physical repetition or taking yourself through the material or skill using your imagination (seriously). Mental self-testing is especially effective for reinforcing newly formed brain connections.

Each of these Six steps is valuable in its own right, and can be applied to various areas of life. Thus, although this chapter is framed in the context of plasticity, each of the protocols has other important applications too. 1'11 explain more as we go. Types of Neuroplasticity Before we explore each step of SDAP, let's get Clear on what we're talking about when we talk about plasticity. All sustained behavioral and cognitive change is the result of plasticity. These changes come in two broad types: adaptive and maladaptive. Adaptive changes are desirable—this is the plasticity that accompanies learning a new language or a new artistic or athletic skill. Maladaptive changes are the ones that make life harder. Consider when a brain injury renders someone unable to produce coherent speech, or a traumatic event leaves someone stricken with PTSD. That's Still plasticity but obviously not the sort you want. These two types of plasticity happen in different ways. Maladaptive plasticity, as in the brain injury I described above, tends to occur fast and is hard to undo. Adaptive plasticity, like learning that new language, takes more effort, and reverts somewhat easily, at least at first. I realize that's not convenient but the sooner we accept that reality, the further along we can all be in our efforts to learn new things. Understanding Why and how maladaptive brain changes occur Will help illustrate how to get the adaptive brain changes that you want, and

make them happen more quickly. Psychologically traumatic events trigger astonishingly fast and stable changes to nervous system wiringu This rewiring happens not just in the brain but in the patterns of brain-to-body and body-to-brain connections, and hormone-control pathways.— The duration of a traumatic event can be very brief—no more than a few seconds— yet bring about persistent or recurring anxiety, sleep disturbances, and physical challenges, like chronic pain,3 rashes,4 gut issues,5 and more, that last for years. This is essentially one trial learning. Something happens and we are (seemingly) forever changed. The evolutionary logic is straightforward: One trial learning from traumatic events helps ensure we avoid similar circumstances in the future. It keeps us safe. How one trial learning happens brings us back to an analogy discussed in chapter 3. Remember the autonomic seesaw? A stress-inducing event or thought causes your autonomic nervous system to increase your sympathetic tone, which makes you alert. That sharpens your focus. If sympathetic tone is too high, however, it feels like anxiety or panic. When we experience a traumatic event, our brains quickly trigger the release of a lot of adrenaline into our bodies and a lot of norepinephrine in our brains.6 Together, these two neuromodulators create all the necessary conditions for plasticity to occur. We're not talking about a bit of normal life stress. We're talking about something you perceive as really scary that causes a large and rapid shift in the neurochemical milieu of the body and brain.

that what is happening is unique and important, and that they need to change to become better equipped for similar circumstances in the future. Another useful way to think about it is that your brain must get the message that there is a gap between its current configuration and the demands you're facing—a deficit of sorts that it needs to overcome. The deficit is resolved by making new brain connections. Now of course your neurons don't talk to each other in words. They don't say, "This is important, and we have a deficit between where we're at and where we need to be, so we need to change." Neurons communicate in the language of chemicals and electricity. So this message is communicated electrochemically, as a shift in your brain and body's neurochemical milieu that in turn alters the amount of firing in the brain circuits that need to change for the desired learning to occur. And when it comes to shifting neurochemical milieus—that is largely the job of neuromodulators. The neuromodulators dopamine, serotonin, adrenaline, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine each serve different purposes, depending on where they are released in your brain or bodyg It's incorrect to say that dopamine alone drives motivation, for instance, or that serotonin controls mood. It's far more varied and nuanced than that. In terms of plasticity, all these neuromodulators can alter the level of electrochemical activity in the circuits I just described. In other words, these neuromodulators can change the amount and the volume that neurons "talk" to each other.

In fact, in the context of plasticity, you can think of a neuromodulator as a microphone lowered over a specific conversation in a crowded stadium. Like a stadium on game day, brains are noisy. They are busy carrying out all kinds of everyday electrochemical duties. The "microphone" makes a conversation louder against the background noise. This is one common way plasticity occurs. The faster and greater the shift in the activity of a given circuit relative to its previous levels, and relative to the background (more electrochemically active), the more likely that circuit Will alter its structure and connections—in other words, the more likely plasticity of the circuit Will occur. It's also true that if neural circuits are quieter (less electrochemically active) against the chatter of usual background brain activity, they can weaken. Different contexts spike the release of different neuromodulators alone or in combination, which amplifies the conversation of the neural circuits active in that context. For example, dopamine is a major neuromodulator released in response to novelty and surprise, which facilitates plasticity for learning and memory.2 And acetylcholine is released at high levels under conditions of heightened focus, but not all over the brain; rather, it's released specifically at the sites in neural circuits that are active. Regardless of which neuromodulator or combination of neuromodulators is released, what happens next is largely the same. Since the brain is homeostatic—that is, it seeks balance— rather than maintain high levels of activity, the neurons that are part of a given conversation

modify themselves so they become more easily active should that context occur again. They may add more receptors to render themselves capable of capturing more neurotransmitters or they may sprout a tiny neurite, an axonal (output) or dendritic (input) branch that becomes part of a new set of synaptic connections with other nearby neuronsn All this changes the threshold for activation of that circuit going forward, and on and on.J2 Voila! That is learningdriven plasticity. Other forms of plasticity involve similar cellular and molecular changes but the conditions that create them are different. SDAP is about creating this situation of specific neural circuits rewiring in specific ways on purpose. The steps involved in this process are designed to help you do just that. Where to Begin Above, I noted that the first step of SDAP is getting alert and the second is getting focused. These two work together in a positive feedback loop. The cool thing is even the mere act of trying to focus shifts us into a slightly more elevated sympathetic tone, which causes our levels of alertness to increase, which then causes activity in the circuits for focusing to increase, which further causes levels of alertness to, you guessed it, increase. For those who struggle with focus, take solace in the fact that the circuits involved with focus are amenable to plasticity too. As you move through the SDAP process described in this chapter, and practice the various protocols here, you'll learn new things, but you'll also get better at focusing, which Will help you to learn more new things, and so on.

There are multiple ways to create the increase in alertness and focus needed for SDAP. 1'11 cover all your options—behavioral, supplement based, pharmacologic—below. But remember this: Alertness and focus are necessary but not suficient for plasticity and learning. To trigger learning, you're also going to have to make errors from genuine attempts, what I refer to as repetitions, or reps. Not deliberate errors, and not half-baked efforts, but rather, errors that emerge from truly exerting yourself to learn new information, new movements, even new modes of thinking. Consider this: If your nervous system can already generate the activity patterns that enable you to do a certain task— perform a dance step, for example, or order coffee in a foreign language—why would it change? It doesn't need to! You're already equipped with the neural circuits to accomplish that task. You need to try, and fail, and try again. This is tough to accept, especially for perfectionists, but all who embrace it thrive. Especially those who come to recognize limbic friction, the slight agitation that accompanies effective learning, as a state to seek, not Shy away from. The importance of making mistakes and trying again doesn't mean you have to toil endlessly. SDAP can be enjoyable. You'll likely experience some limbic friction but guess what? Once you learn to expect it, and you realize that it helps not hinders your ability to learn, you too Will be seeking it out. You may be wondering "Why all these conditions for plasticity? Isn't there a plasticity pill?" No. As I mentioned earlier in this introduction, plasticity is energetically expensive.

sequence is more important than any one tool listed here. This Will be an important reframing for a lot of people. I mentioned that there wasn't a pill for plasticity, but people love to think about what they can take to increase neuromodulator levels to heighten focus. Adderall, energy drinks, nicotine, modafinil, microdoses of psilocybin, et cetera, are used by many people working in business, tech, sports performance, finance circles, and beyond to try to focus and learn better. The use of such stimulants is widespread on college campuses and among high school students in the US,J-3 and millions of adults use them daily too. Their widespread use merely speaks to how hard most people find it to focus intensely enough and push through limbic friction. I'm not judging anyone. For example, I, like most adults in the US,J4 use caffeine daily to increase focus. I occasionally rely on other pharmacologic tools for focus too. In this chapter, 1'11 cover the popular as well as the rarely discussed ones. That all being said, the main focus here is behavioral tools. They may not seem as sexy, but many rival the pharmacologic tools. It truly doesn't matter what you use to get alert and focused, as long as it's safe. If you opt to use nicotine or modafinil or meditation or good 01' sleep and hydration, those obviously have different safety profiles. You can use white noise or various sound tones.J5 These all have data to support them in the context of focus and learning. You can cycle different tools in and out, by the day or by the month. The point is: You

have choices. Think of them as tools in your SDAP arsenal. Stick with It We know a lot more about plasticity now than we did twenty-five or even just five years ago. Prior to the 2000s the widely held belief—even among neuroscience researchers—was that the opportunity for adaptive plasticity mostly closes after age twenty-five.L6 That idea is now dead. We know people can rewire their brains and learn throughout their lifespans.UZ Also mostly dead is the idea that learning-associated plasticity involves the addition of new neurons. Plasticity in humans is almost exclusively the consequence of changes to existing neural circuits, not adding new neurons to those circuits.J-g And yet, the results you can achieve when you incorporate the best of what we know about SDAP can be extraordinary. Here is an overview of SDAP, once more: • Get alert. • Get and stay focused. • Maintain a state of urgency. • Embrace errors that arise from genuine attempts. • Rest. • Repeat your performance. I've listed these again because the steps and the sequence are non-negotiable. Not because I say so, but because that's how our neuroplasticity works. There are things you can do to accelerate the process: all the tools I mentioned above (and more), along with micro-pauses, post-learningbout NSDR, adjusted sleep protocols, and hypnosis. I cover all these in the pages that follow. I began this chapter with this basic process because it can be applied to learning anything. Similar to exercise, SDAP is not easy. But with time, each step becomes familiar. If you think of SDAP this way—as a process that consistently leads to a desired end—it can become a pleasure.
LEARNING PROTOCOL Shift into a State of Alertness and Focus
WHAT TO DO

• Getting alert and focused is the first step in SDAP. You have to be in a state of elevated autonomic (sympathetic) arousal, but not stressed. • Use tools to help you achieve this state. Such tOOlS are many and varied, and fall into three general categories: • Foundational • Behavioral • Pharmacological • Put your Phone away. You may think you have an issue with getting focused, but it's likely that you are distracted by something in your surroundings—the smartphone being the major culprit. Studies show that even just having your Phone in the same room in a bag behind or under your chair reduces your ability to focus on cognitive tasks and/or increases the energy that it takes.12
HOW IT WORKS
You might be thinking "Why would anyone need a protocol for focus?"

oversized motorcycle helmet designed to be worn while seated at a desk, created by industrial design company Hochu rayu.24 The rationale was the same, all that time later: Block out peripheral vision and outside noise to help people focus. The Helmfon, as you might imagine, also did not gain traction. Even if it had, the advent of social media and other online activities essentially moved the outside noise of the entire world directly into one's central field of view. So much for helmets. Other long-used tools include nonamphetamine stimulants such as caffeine, which blocks adenosine receptors in the brain that would otherwise trigger sleepiness, and nicotine, which triggers the release of several neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter. The use of caffeine in the form of tea or coffee dates back more than two thousand years. But coffee and tea didn't become popular in Europe until the seventeenth century, the result of invasions and trade.25 Today, approximately 90 percent of the world's adults—that's estimated as more than five billion people (!)—drink caffeine every single day. Later 1'11 explain how to use caffeine specifically to enhance focus, but meanwhile those stats reveal that caffeine is the most popular drug on the planet by a huge margin. (If you're wondering, alcohol and nicotine are in a distant second and third place, respectively.) Nicotine, mostly in oral forms like pouches, gum, and mints, has made a big comeback as a focus aid in recent years. I recently gave a talk to several thousand undergraduate men and women at an East Coast university and asked the auditorium for a show of hands of "who in here

takes nicotine daily?" About 30 percent of them raised their hands. (In a more private setting— a smaller group of about fifty male students— about two-thirds said they use nicotine two or more times per day every day.) This is obviously not a controlled study, nor did I count each hand, but even if these are artificially high estimates, it's Still pretty shocking. Or is it? Nicotine is an unusual stimulant because it makes people alert but calm—a highly desirable state for learning. Unless smoked, vaped, dipped, or snuffed, nicotine does not cause cancer, but it is highly addictive and it raises blood pressure.26 Later, 1'11 explain how, assuming you're Okay with the risks, nicotine can be used to enhance focus. There are a few safer alternatives, some of which work through the same mechanisms. And there are the amphetamines. First synthesized in Romania in the late 1880s, amphetamines are compounds that increase levels of some of the key neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter, like norepinephrine and dopamine.ZZ These stimulants were initially marketed in the 1930s as a treatment for narcolepsy, but soon hit the college scene when research showed a link with increased scores on intelligence tests. They were also investigated for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and as appetite suppressants starting even back then.22 A decade later, both German and Allied forces used amphetamines during World War II to stay awake and alert.30 Recreational use of amphetamines exploded in general popularity starting in the 1950s, partly due to a surplus from World War II. By the 1960s, there was an

epidemic of amphetamine dependency and abuse in the United Statesn They were made illegal for non-prescription use in the early 1970s, classified in the same way as cocaine and morphine, and their use dropped. That is, until the FDA approved amphetamines for the treatment of ADHD in 1996.32 Drugs marketed for ADHD like Adderall, Vyvanse, et cetera, are amphetamines, and they work quite well to increase alertness and focus. Current exact rates are hard to come by, but it seems that up to 35 percent of college students use stimulants at some point during their undergraduate years.33 For people without a genuine clinical need for amphetamines, their use can be problematic. They are effective for helping people complete work that relies on skills they already have, but far less effective for learning new skills. They are lousy for contemplative thinking, are very addictive. That's too, and creative endeavors. And they habit forming, and in many cases the history. And while getting and staying focused has always been hard, it seems it's now harder than ever. The good news is that accessing a state of focus necessary for SDAP is possible for anyone. It starts with understanding the states of mind and body you're after. You'll recall that negative experiences automatically set off the learning process. No coffee, no tutor, no motivational video or mantra required. The fast, massive increase in sympathetic tone caused by adrenaline and norepinephrine ramps up activity in relevant brain circuits. It's proof that if the right electrochemical systems get triggered, we all have the capacity to focus. Again, I'm

It's where one person places their hands out, palms up, and you put your hands on theirs, palms down. The person with palms up flips their hands over to try and tap the top of your hands before you can pull away. You don't know when they Will make their move. You're alert and focused, anticipating something Will happen. Learn to recognize that state. That's the ideal level of autonomic arousal for a learning bout. With a bit of practice you'll be able to sense when your autonomic arousal is climbing too high or dropping too low, and keep yourself in that ideal state. In other words, you learn to get better at entering the learning process. Is Being Focused the Same as Being in a Flow State? No. Don't confuse this state with a flow state. In flow states we forget the rest of the world (and even ourselves), and we do things as if on autopilot.32 Flow states are ideal for task performance—executing cognitive and motor skills we have already mastered. We don't learn in flow states, we implement what we already learned. The person who first described flow states—the Hungarian psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi —accurately described this feeling as when the challenge of a task is matched with your existing skill level, not too easy, nor too hard.. just challenging enough to engage you and "an absolute sense of control."40 That last part—"an absolute sense of control"—means your brain already has the neural circuits in place that it needs to execute the task. And as we discussed

above, that means no rewiring... no plasticity is triggered, and no learning occurs. To trigger plasticity and start learning, you must push past your current abilities. You have to get stumped, miss the mark, and most importantly, you have to feel the agitation of making errors. Recognize that as limbic friction, and seek it out. Ask any elite performer how they got so good at their craft and they Will tell you, "Practice, lots of practice." But there are two kinds of practice. There are the hours upon hours spent drilling what we already know how to do and there is the practice of pushing ourselves to learn new skills. The latter is accomplished by making errors through genuine attempts. As the great Twyla Tharp, world-renowned choreographer and dancer, put it, "The more you fail in private, the less you Will fail in public."41 Twyla understands that elite performance requires genuine attempts —failing and failing again (and again), until the gap between one's goal and actual performance is reduced to zero. The Learning State The experiments that perhaps best illustrate the vital role of focused attention in learning come from the work of neuroscientist Mike Merzenich, PhD, and his lab at University of California, San Francisco.42 The studies were done in the 1990s using monkeys and later adapted to studies in humans. The monkeys were trained to place their fingers on a rotating cylinder that had both coarse and fine bumps laid out in rows across its surface.

The monkeys quickly learned that if they detected a difference between the coarse bumps and the fine bumps, they earned a reward. To signal when they noticed that difference, they used their other hand to move a joystick. Over time, the researchers made the task harder by making the difference in the bumps progressively smaller, which required more focus from the monkeys. Not only did the monkeys learn to perform the harder task, but the researchers observed significant changes in the brain areas representing sensations in the fingers that were touching the cylinder. In other words, they observed plasticity associated with that learning. These were adult monkeys, too, showing that plasticity was not just confined to developmental critical periods as had long been believed. That was interesting but it was just the beginning of the story. In other studies from Merzenich, monkeys had to learn to discriminate between different sound tones. In that case the regions of the brain responsible for hearing changed. Perhaps not surprising, except that the monkeys were experiencing bumps on their fingers at the same time they heard the tones. So Why did only the auditory areas of the brain change? Because the monkeys received rewards only for learning sound tones, so that's what they focused on. Together, these two sets of experiments showed that mere experience doesn't cause neuroplasticity. Learning-associated brain plasticity only occurs in the circuits associated with where our attention is placed. Since those landmark studies, there have been thousands of experiments exploring

the participants were instructed to pay attention to. The finding leads to a profound insight: that the plasticity they experienced was tied to the act of looking for something and not solely to the success offinding that something. As the authors concluded, "Learning Will occur only in those neurons that are activated by the stimulus and that are at the same time relevant for the task. Which neurons are relevant [for neuroplasticity] is dictated by the mechanism or strategy used for task performance (and not merely a stimulusresponse correlation)." These results, along with the earlier studies mentioned here, point to the crucial role of focus in plasticity and learning. Which brings us to the common saying "fire together, wire together."42 People often use this phrase to capture the idea that habits form from neurons being activated at nearly the exact same time. The thinking goes that neurons firing simultaneously or one after the other causes them to become wired together, which Will lead them to readily fire together in the future. But the term "fire together, wire together" is actually unrelated to the kind of learning we are talking about in this chapter—achieving new skills, developing new behavioral patterns, et cetera. This is not a trivial point. This phrase is often attached to the false notion that people can learn when in passive or semi-engaged states. It implies that we can simply expose kids to music to enrich their brain. Not sos It also implies that simply reading or doing something repeatedly is enough to create new brain patterns. Alas, not so. Oh and the "fire together, wire together" phrase is constantly misattributed to psychologist Donald

Hebb when in fact it was Carla Shatz, the developmental neurobiologist, who said it first— in the context of developmental brain wiring, not learning.50 The point is this: Whether young or Old, ifwe want to learn, we need to focus intensely on new information, or in the case of cognitive or motor skills, on our attempt to perform them. The good news is that with the right tools and a little practice, anyone can access focus... and learn. Tools for Focus As I mentioned in the introduction to this protocol, we humans have long sought tools to make this endeavor easier. Here's where science puts us today. There are three categories of tools to get alert and focused. Foundational Behavioral Pharmacological The tools offered here can be used for learning bouts, as described above, or even for what I call work sessions—time when you're not necessarily tackling new information or skills, but grappling with some work or physical challenge that simply requires intense focus. FOUNDATIONAL TOOLS FOR FOCUS These tools are the bedrock upon which all the other suggestions in this protocol depend. Without them, the rest of the tools in this protocol Will be far less effective. Get the foundational tools right, and you'll greatly amplify the potency of all others you opt to use.

Foundational Tool 1: Sleep In chapter 1 when I said that sleep is the foundation of mental health, physical health, and performance, that included learning of all kinds. When we do not get enough quality sleep, or if our sleep timing is altered by more than an hour or two from our normal schedule, our levels of alertness get harder to regulate and so focusing becomes an even bigger challenge. Thus, aim to get adequate sleep using the protocols in chapter 1. (See Sleep Protocols 1—6 for a reminder on the basics.) Foundational Tool 2: NSDR If you've had less than adequate sleep and you're trying to lock in on a learning bout, consider doing ten, twenty, or, if possible, thirty minutes of non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) at some point prior to starting that learning bout. NSDR, while not a replacement for sleep, is your best bet to restore mental and physical vigor if you didn't get enough sleep. As mentioned in Sleep Protocol 8, NSDR is preferable to naps, because it doesn't create sleep inertia so you won't finish a session feeling groggy, nor does it disrupt your normal sleep schedule. A short nap of thirty minutes or less can also restore mental and physical vigor, but midday napping for more than thirty minutes can really mess up your nighttime sleep. Refer to Sleep Protocol 7 for best practices. Foundational Tool 3: Stress Control The other key to an effective learning bout is to make sure you don't show up in a state of excessively high sympathetic tone, or what we

commonly call stress. Stressing about something other than what you're trying to learn steals your focus. If you're worrying about your to-do list, it's hard to focus on learning a new song on the guitar. And stressing about what you're trying to learn prevents you from staying in the alert but calm state you're after. Chapter 3 provides tools you can use when you aren't actively engaged in a learning bout—as well as tools you can use during a learning bout, such as the physiological sigh. Both types of tools are effective to help maintain your level of arousal near the peak of the inverted U-shape curve that is ideal for learning. Foundational Tool 4: Nutrition If you're even mildly dehydrated, your focus won't be at its best.5-J Drink water and, if you need to, add some electrolytes, which aids the rehydration process. The same goes for your blood sugar levels—make sure yours are relatively stable by not reaching for sugary foods when you know you want to be focused. Chapter 4 described how to eat to fuel your body for all types of activity, and that includes learning bouts and work sessions. Those protocols offered guidelines, but there are options for how you adapt them for your schedule when it comes to learning. For example, in the first two to three hours of my day, I focus best if I'm fasted. I make sure I'm hydrated, and that I'm caffeinated, too, but unless I wake up especially hungry (a rarity for me), I don't eat yet. If I already exercised that morning, however, I eat, and then I start work.

can significantly improve your ability to focus. Some assist the transition into a state of focus, and others help you stay there. Behavioral Tool 1: Meditation Meditation can take many forms. One shown to improve focus is as follows: Set aside about ten to twenty minutes, sit or lie down, close your eyes, and direct your mental attention to the location between your eyes, or concentrate on your breathing, or both. As you strive to maintain those points of focus, thoughts, sensations, and outside noises inevitably distract you. Keep redirecting your attention back to the location between your eyes and/or breathing, over and over again, as many times as needed until the allotted time elapses. Behavioral Tool 3: 40 Hertz Binaural Beats, 20 Hertz Oscillatory Induction, and White, Brown, and Pink Noise The use of sound as a tool for focus is all about entrainment, or the matching of our internal rhythms to an external sensory event—in these cases, the frequency of sound waves. You may remember the term entrainment from chapter 1 and chapter 5. There, I talked about entraining your circadian rhythm to light, for example, by viewing bright light in the first hour after waking up. There are also ways to entrain to events in the outside world. For example, when you exercise at roughly the same time of day, you experience an increase in catecholamines and certain hormones at that time. Then after about three days or so, you automatically start to feel an increase in energy just prior to when you usually exercise. Entrainment works based on your nervous system's expectation of certain things happening.

Sound waves can entrain our brain, too, and they do so very quickly. When we hear certain frequencies or rhythms, our brain starts to entrain to the predictable features in the sound by our neurons firing in regular fashion. Scientists have figured out how to leverage that and have created specific sound patterns that increase brain activity in areas that underlie focused states. One example is binaural beats. Two distinct frequencies of sounds are played in each ear. When that happens, a cluster of neurons in your brainstem called the medial superior olivary nucleus performs a subtraction of the two frequencies. So if a 400 hertz (Hz) sound arrives at one ear and 440 Hz at the other ear, it leads you to perceive a 40 Hz beat. That sound frequency, in particular, has been shown to improve levels of focus, and even certain forms of memory.6 The precise mechanisms for this are Still being parsed but there is evidence that 40 Hz sound can do this in part by causing release of acetylcholine from the medial superior olivary nucleus and the release of dopamine in the striatum, a brain area involved in movement and motivated attention. Some evidence even shows that 40 Hz sounds can trigger the brain circuits involved in focus and memory to enter what are called gamma oscillation states, a pattern of neural activity that is favorable for learning.é6 (Interestingly, there is parallel evidence that activating these circuits using clinical devices may also help offset some of the early symptoms of age-related cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease.6-Z)

Behavioral Tool 6: Proper Breathing Sleep apnea is a condition where people under-breathe during sleep. Nasal obstructions, excessive weight, and certain medications cause it. If you snore, there's a good chance you have sleep apnea. The result? Your brain is deprived of oxygen at night. Sleep apnea is a dangerous condition, because the health impacts creep up over time—causing fatigue, cognitive impairments, heart issues, and more" Some of these can be reversed with tools to correct breathing while you sleep, but longlasting impairments can occur. Why am I discussing sleep apnea in a protocol on focus? Because many people have daytime apnea that impairs their focus too.Z2 Daytime apnea is when you hold your breath while working. Chronic mouth breathers experience the same. When your brain doesn't get enough oxygen, you get tired and you can't focus. To feel alert and focus intensely, you need to fix sleep and any daytime apnea. Luckily, it's easy to do. First, make sure you're breathing through your nose anytime you don't have to speak, eat, or exercise hard. Second, learn to breathe with your diaphragm, also known as

belly breathing, in which your belly expands as you inhale. This approach increases the amount of oxygen in the blood and promotes a more relaxed state. You'll be amazed what a difference that Will make for your energy levels and focus. Check right now. If you're mouth breathing, switch to nasal breathing. Does your belly move out as you inhale and move in as you exhale through your nose? If so, great, you're nasal diaphragmatic breathing. If you're having trouble, imagine inhaling through your nose as if trying to direct the air backward—in other words, think about drawing the air "in and back" through your nose at an angle parallel to the roof of your mouth, as opposed to inhaling "up" your nostrils toward the top of your head. I know that sounds weird, but try it. You'll notice that you immediately shift. And no, you don't have to think about your breathing all day. After two to three breaths done consciously that way, it Will carry on reflexively. Nasal diaphragmatic breathing in the daytime also helps you default to the right breathing pattern when you sleep, which can help offset sleep apnea, so it's a twofer. A few other issues with breathing to address here. If you have a badly deviated septum or challenged nasal breathing brought about by cartilage growth in your nasal passages, you need to fix that. Extreme cases of nasal passage collapse or other blockage may require surgery. People can often achieve some results from wearing a magnetic nose bridge for a few hours a day and/or at night.

Behavioral Tool 7: Cyclic Hyperventilation Cyclic hyperventilation might sound familiar, but there's new context for this powerful tool. It's quite simple. You hyperventilate. Intentionally. Not a bunch of quick shallow breaths—that's panting! Instead do ten to twenty cycles of a big deep inhale through your nose, using diaphragmatic breathing as described in the section above, and exhale, letting the air passively "fall out" from your mouth. You don't have to heave into the inhale to get the effect you're seeking. Work up to it gradually, and focus on long, diaphragmatic inhales through the nose. Increase the vigor after a few repetitions. After ten to twenty breaths this way, you Will reliably feel much more alert. As covered in chapter 3, you can spike your levels of adrenaline and norepinephrine and dopamine—the so-called catecholamines— and thereby increase your alertness and focus, by breathing in this specific way. It works by causing increased discard of carbon dioxide, which is called hypocapnia, and increased alkalinity of your blood pH, which is called alkalosis. That in turn triggers fast and significant increases in adrenaline and norepinephrine release in your body and brain. If you think breathing to shift catecholamine levels is not very potent, think again. This tool works fast and extremely well to increase alertness, so you can focus on whatever task lies before you. It's a causal relationship. In experiments where people hyperventilated through an air mask with artificially elevated C02, their epinephrine and norepinephrine levels

did not increase, nor did they achieve alkalosis. This tells us it's not just the mechanics of deep breathing, it's about increased discard of C02. By the way, that is Why people having a panic attack are told to breathe into a paper bag; it's to encourage them to re-breathe the C02 they expelled, and bring their epinephrine and norepinephrine back to baseline. When you do cyclic hyperventilation, you won't have a panic attack as long as you pay attention to your autonomic state as you do. If you feel alert after ten breaths, stop. If not, do ten more breaths. If you want, complete twenty breaths, then take a long exhale and hold your breath for ten to Sixty seconds until you feel the gasp reflex, and then start another round of cyclic hyperventilation. When you're as alert as you want to be, resume normal nasal diaphragmatic breathing. Sure, cyclic hyperventilation looks a little wacky but so what? It costs nothing, and it works. It may also have benefits for your immune system. Just don't ever do it in or near water, or while driving, because when your C02 is low, the impulse to breathe is delayed. People have drowned practicing this breathing pattern as a way to extend how long they can hold their breath underwater. Behavioral Tool 8: Deliberate Cold Exposure Deliberate cold exposure works very well to increase alertness and focus for hours afterward. catecholamines—and it does it within seconds. That is not the idea here. This is: Try thirty seconds to three minutes of deliberate cold exposure, then shower and start your learning bout or work session. It's about using deliberate cold exposure to create a long-lasting window of moderate catecholamine increase. Depending on the duration of the cold exposure, the increase in alertness and focus can last for many hours afterward. The challenge is there is no one-size-fitsall protocol for this one because people's cold tolerance varies. Refer to Stress Control Protocol 2 for more information. If you're using a shower, get all the way under the water. And yes, put your hands in the water, too, unless you need to grip the sides for safety. The water should be cold, but shouldn't cause pain. WHAT TO DO

It's constantly trying to make causal inferences: "If I do A, then B seems to happen immediately afterward... If I don't do X, then Y happens a few hours later..." When you are awake, your nervous system is running a ceaseless if-then analysis of you and your actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of others and their actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of the world around you, and on and on. actions leads to a successful outcome, it starts to shift the pattern of neural firing that occurred from your conscious awareness into your implicit motor memory. Your cerebellum is kind of like that tennis coach in this regard, except unlike a coach that observes you and makes educated guesses as to what you need to do in order to improve, your cerebellum has full access to both your inner and outer workings: the angles of your limbs and joints, the speed and stretch of your muscles; it knows when you blinked relative to your maximum effort, your level of autonomic arousal, et cetera. Thus, your cerebellum is also uniquely suited to be your coach because of both the specificity and the interconnectedness of its wiring. Different cerebellar neurons respond to the movement of different parts of the body, even your eyes and lips and tongue. It also encodes how movement of one body area changes the movement of all the others. If you consciously adjust the angle of your elbow and it improves your serve, your cerebellum registers the many other changes that accompanied the elbow adjustment and then makes sure they become part of your serve "motor program" going forward. If your elbow angle adjustment makes things worse, your cerebellum registers that too. With repeated effort, your brain eventually stamps down the exact motor program needed to serve the ball properly.
